Everything that exists really can appear: the natural world and the human world—the historical, technical, social, and political world—in every aspect, from every angle, and in every possible combination.
But things that do not exist in reality can also appear: √2, Chichikov, God, the dative case, a dragon, and so on.
Even what does not exist at all can appear in a certain sense.
What I call “nothingness” or “non-being,” for example, in some sense “appears” to me precisely as what cannot be spoken of, what cannot be known, and so on—even though it does not exist.
Return to our example of the birch.
The birch I am actually looking at now “appears” to me. But so does the birch I looked at ten years ago.
So too does the “birch in general,” which no one could ever literally look at, but which the botanist describes.
Even the word “birch,” considered as such by a philologist, can be said to “appear.”
The phenomenon of the birch can therefore take the form of sensory perception, memory, spoken discourse about it, and so forth.

And anything that appears to a human being can appear in any number of ways: in sensory perception, memory, imagination, human discourse, a mathematical formula, a painting, a musical work, and so on.

A birch manifests itself to human beings not only when an ordinary person sees it, but when a scientist talks about it—whether a botanist, biologist, chemist, physicist, mathematician, or someone else—or when an artist or poet depicts it.

Finally, anything can “appear” in any way to anyone: to ordinary people and scientists, to the mad and the “sane,” to children and old people, to people of our own age and people of the Stone Age, and so on.
An appearance or phenomenon is therefore anything that “manifests itself” in some way to some person.
Every phenomenon is consequently always an appearance to a particular person.
But what we call the “phenomenon” is not the person to whom it appears, nor the means through which it appears. It is simply what appears.
Suppose a birch appears to an ordinary person through an actual sensory perception.
In this case, the phenomenon is neither the person nor his perception. It is the birch.
But is it the birch “in itself”?
No. It is precisely the birch as it appears to this particular person in this particular sensory perception.
The ordinary person thinks he is dealing with the birch itself.
The philosopher knows that he is dealing with a birch as it appears to him through his perception.
So although the ordinary person—and the scientist—speaks about the birch, he completely forgets that it is appearing in a certain way to a certain person.
The philosopher, speaking about the same tree, continually remembers this.
For that reason the philosopher does not simply speak of the “birch,” but of the phenomenon or appearance of the birch.
He knows that this tree appears in a certain way to a certain person.

So even if, for the moment, he sets aside the question “to whom does it appear, and how?”, he still remembers that his account of the phenomenon “birch” is incomplete and must eventually be supplemented by an account of how it appears and to whom.
Phenomenology is the philosophical discourse or science that studies phenomena as phenomena.
That is, it is a discourse that remembers not only that phenomena make something appear, but also that they make it appear in a particular way and to a particular person.
It is “philosophy” in the broad sense because it describes and studies its object—the phenomenon—without abstracting from anything.
But to understand what is distinctive about Phenomenology, we must remember that it is not the only philosophical science.
Alongside it there is “philosophy” in the narrower sense: systematic Philosophy.
If we can study the phenomenon as phenomenon, we can also move, so to speak, beyond its limits and ask what lies “behind” it.
What must reality itself be like for this phenomenon or appearance to be possible?

Or again: if we use the word world (cosmos) for everything that exists in any way—naturally, historically and really, or ideally—what must the world be like for it to appear to a human being living within it exactly as it actually appears?
Using Kant’s language, we can define this properly philosophical theme as the question of the “condition of possibility of phenomena” (Bedingung der Möglichkeit der Erscheinungen).
To understand what is meant here, we can use an analogy from science, especially chemistry and physics.
An ordinary person—or a botanist—may say that a cornflower is dark blue and be satisfied with that.
The physicist and chemist ask a different question:
What must this cornflower be like “in reality” for it to appear blue?
The chemist may answer that it appears blue because it contains certain pigments: chemical bodies composed of supposedly elementary constituents or “atoms.”

The physicist goes further. He argues that the chemical atoms must possess a particular physical structure allowing them to emit or reflect “blue light”—that is, in reality, electromagnetic oscillations of a certain frequency—for the cornflower to appear blue.
Both the chemist and the physicist therefore move beyond what is revealed to the ordinary person’s “naked eye,” and the physicist goes beyond what is available to the chemist’s observation as well.

If the ordinary person is looking at the scenery on the stage of a theatre, the chemist is inspecting the backstage area, while the physicist is examining the machinery that makes the backstage effects possible.
Like the chemist and physicist, the systematic philosopher also goes, so to speak, behind the stage observed by the phenomenologist.
The phenomenologist sees the appearances. The philosopher asks about their “causes.”
But we must remember that this is only an analogy.
Physics and chemistry are no more philosophical than naive perception—or botanical perception.
So the “cause” sought by the philosopher has nothing in common with the cause sought by the physicist or chemist.
The philosopher seeks the cause of a phenomenon as phenomenon.
The scientist seeks the cause of the “thing itself,” independently of how it appears and of the person to whom it appears.
The physicist, for example, does not ask how electromagnetic vibrations themselves “appear,” or to whom they appear.
The philosopher knows that they too must appear in some particular way to some particular person.
For the philosopher, therefore, the chemical and physical causes used to explain the blue colour of the flower are themselves just as much appearances or phenomena as the cornflower.
So when the philosopher searches for the “cause” of phenomena, he cannot find it in any science, because science itself is only one phenomenon among others.
Science explains some phenomena by means of other phenomena while forgetting that it is itself dealing only with phenomena.
The philosopher’s world or cosmos, by contrast—the world that must serve as the “cause” or “condition of possibility” of phenomena—must explain phenomena precisely as phenomena.
It must be such that not only what appears is possible, but also how it appears and to whom it appears.

Through a discourse or “science of the world”—a cosmo-logy—the philosopher must show what the existing world must be like not only in order to exist, but in order to appear to human beings exactly as it actually appears.
This philosophical “world” therefore includes not only whatever underlies nature, but whatever underlies human beings and their cognition of nature.

A philosophical description of the world—Cosmology—must therefore be just as concrete, complete, and non-abstract as the philosophical description of all possible phenomena of that world—that is, as Phenomenology.

The “world” of philosophy includes not only nature but also humanity, together with everything human beings have created throughout history through both practical historical activity and theoretical activity.
It therefore includes not only the real technical world, but also the “ideal” world of discourse.
So the theme or object of Cosmology is not a world separated from humanity, but a world containing humanity—or, what amounts to the same thing, human beings in the world.
Phenomenology, by contrast, studies the world in the human being: the way the world in the cosmological sense—that is, the human being in the world—“manifests” itself to human beings.
In other words, it studies how “the human being in the world” reveals both the world and itself to itself.
If we like, the cosmological world is itself also a “phenomenon,” since it too “manifests” itself in some way to someone.
But it manifests itself only philosophically, and only to the philosopher as philosopher.

A phenomenon in the narrower sense, by contrast, can manifest itself in any way to anyone—including to the philosopher insofar as the philosopher is not merely a philosopher but also an ordinary human being.

It is therefore better not to extend the word phenomenon to the world of Cosmology, especially because this world already includes both the way in which it appears and the person to whom it appears—that is, philosophy and the philosopher.
Cosmology therefore differs fundamentally from Phenomenology in both theme and object.
Phenomenology studies phenomena. Cosmology asks what the world must be like in order to appear as it does—to human beings and therefore, ultimately, to itself, since the world contains human beings.
But philosophical questioning is not exhausted by this cosmological question.
Just as we can ask about the “cause” of phenomena, we can ask about the “cause” of that cause—the “cause” of the world or cosmos.
And because this world actually exists, the question conceals another question: the question of the “cause” of existence or actuality itself.
This “cause” is called being itself (on, ontos).
We can say that actuality or the existence of the world is a form, appearance, or mode of being of Being.
Likewise, a phenomenon or appearance is the form, aspect, or mode in which real and ideal actuality exists.
If actuality—natural, human, and ideal—is the “condition of possibility of phenomena,” then Being as Being (ontos on) is the “condition of possibility of actuality or existence.”
A discourse or science of the existing, actual world—Cosmology—must therefore be supplemented by a discourse or science of Being: an onto-logy.

In other words, we must also ask what Being itself must be like in order to exist as it actually does—that is, in order to be this world or cosmos that manifests itself in the way it actually manifests itself to human beings and therefore, ultimately, to itself.

We can return once more to our analogy and say that Ontology stands in relation to Cosmology and Phenomenology somewhat as physics stands in relation to chemistry and to the ordinary content of nature that anyone can observe.
But here it is even clearer that this is only an analogy.
Ontology has nothing in common with physics or, more generally, with any non-philosophical science.

In the case of Cosmology, some misunderstanding is still possible because many sciences deal with the world. We therefore have to distinguish “scientific” Cosmology from philosophical Cosmology by pointing out that science studies the world very differently from philosophy: abstractly rather than concretely.
Ontology is different. Only philosophical Ontology speaks of Being as Being, so there is no comparable danger of confusion.
This is not the place to define in detail the object and theme of Ontology or Cosmology. We need only examine their relation to Phenomenology.
Because Ontology and Cosmology both deal not with phenomena but with their “causes,” they together form a single whole distinct from Phenomenology.
We call this whole systematic Philosophy, or Philosophy in the narrower sense.
If we move out of Phenomenology, then Cosmology must come first after it.
